---
title: "Discussion"
---

This thesis was concerned with the treatment of missing data in predictor variables in small-sample multilevel models with group-mean predictors. It focused on a reduced setting with a single continuous predictor which was included at level 1 as an individual-level predictor and at level 2 as a manifest group-mean predictor, within a random intercept model. In addition, one auxiliary variable at level 2 was included to explain missingness under a MAR mechanism, without being directly related to the outcome. The analytical setup aimed to mirror common applied practice, combining default prior specifications with widely recommended small-sample procedures such as REML estimation. There is still limited literature addressing the combined challenges of multilevel data, small sample sizes, and missing data. Against this background, focusing on a simplified setting allowed for a controlled investigation of method performance under systematically varied conditions. This thesis investigated the performance of two modern missingness approaches, multiple imputation and a fully Bayesian approach, alongside a comparison with listwise deletion as a commonly used software default.  

The results indicate a trade-off between bias and interval width when comparing multiple imputation and the fully Bayesian approach. In settings with low ICC and default prior specifications, the fully Bayesian approach may offer advantages over multiple imputation with respect to bias, with differences persisting even at comparatively larger cluster sizes in the present design. Although multiple imputation can be understood as an approximate Bayesian procedure, as it relies on draws from the posterior predictive distribution [e.g., @endersbook, p. 299; @SG2002], the present results highlight that conceptual similarities between methods do not necessarily imply equivalent performance under specific modeling choices. In particular, prior specification played an important role in this context, as indicated by the sensitivity analysis. When reasonable prior information is available for level-2 variance components, incorporating this information through weakly informative priors can reduce bias in multiple imputation while holding coverage at a nominal level.  
One aspect of multiple imputation that was specifically investigated in this thesis was the behavior of inference based on uncorrected versus small-sample-adjusted degrees of freedom. The findings suggest that, in this setting, standard Rubin’s rules already yield approximately valid inference, and that additional small-sample corrections may not be necessary. This is somewhat surprising, as it is commonly recommended to use an appropriate sampling distribution in small samples to avoid overly narrow confidence intervals; a recommendation which also applies to multilevel analyses [@kenwardroger; @schaalje] and within multiple imputation [@barnard]. However, confidence intervals are influenced by multiple sources of uncertainty beyond the degrees-of-freedom approximation alone. In particular, REML estimation was used for analyzing the imputed data sets. Compared to ML, REML typically yields larger estimates of level-2 variance components, which have been shown to improve variance estimation in small samples [@elff; @mcneishstaple14]. As these variance components directly affect standard errors, this may have contributed to wider intervals and thus higher coverage. In addition, multiple imputation was performed using joint modeling via `jomo`. Previous work has shown that inverse Wishart priors with few degrees of freedom, as implemented in `jomo`, can introduce additional variability into fixed-effect estimates [@audigier]. Overall, the present standard MI setup performed well with respect to coverage in the random intercept model with group-mean predictors, which may be reassuring for applied researchers relying on default degrees-of-freedom specifications.  
In terms of implementation, both fully Bayesian estimation and multiple imputation allow the inclusion of auxiliary variables, which were also part of the present setup. In multiple imputation, their inclusion is typically well-documented and supported by standard workflows. In fully Bayesian approaches, however, incorporating auxiliary variables without altering the analysis model requires additional modeling decisions that are less explicitly supported by standardized workflows and software guidance and may therefore not be immediately apparent without prior methodological experience. The choice between approaches is likely to depend not only on statistical performance but also on the research context and analytical goals. Multiple imputation may be advantageous in settings involving multiple analyses (e.g., multiple outcomes), where standardized workflows and comparability across analyses are desired, as completed data sets can be reused and shared. In contrast, fully Bayesian approaches may be particularly useful in cumulative research settings, where prior information can be updated across studies and evidence can be formally integrated over time. However, these distinctions are not absolute, and both approaches can, in principle, be adapted to a wide range of analytical scenarios.

This simulation study comes with several limitations. Firstly, the simulation design had a restricted scope, and the results can therefore only be interpreted within this specific setting, characterized by a random intercept model, a single continuous predictor, a relatively weak MAR mechanism, manifest group means, a moderate ICC range, and a small but not extremely small number of clusters. Future research should extend this design to more complex data-generating processes, including models with multiple predictors, random slopes, categorical variables, non-normal outcomes, heteroscedastic or unbalanced data, interaction effects, three- and more level models, and stronger or alternative missingness mechanisms.  
In addition, key modeling choices were held constant across conditions. These included the use of default prior specifications, joint modeling for multiple imputation, REML estimation, and a correctly specified analysis model consistent with the data-generating process. Only a single degrees-of-freedom correction was investigated. Future research could systematically vary these components to disentangle their relative contributions to estimation performance, including different prior specifications, estimation methods (ML versus REML), imputation frameworks (joint versus fully conditional specification), and small-sample corrections (e.g., Kenward–Roger, m − l − 1). This would help clarify the behavior of multiple imputation in comparison with a fully Bayesian approach and identify the conditions under which small-sample corrections for degrees of freedom are beneficial [see @mcneishgrowth] and those under which, as in the present case, they may not be necessary.
Prior specification is particularly important in small samples. While the present study only examined this aspect in a sensitivity analysis, future work could systematically investigate the impact of different prior choices in both multiple imputation and Bayesian estimation in few-cluster missing data problems. For example, data-dependent priors have been proposed as a way to mitigate small-sample bias [@mcneishpriors] and could be further investigated.  
Furthermore, two distinct software packages were used for multiple imputation and Bayesian estimation. In particular, the default priors in `mdmb` allow for greater variability in parameter estimates than those implemented in `jomo`. Using a common software framework for both approaches, as for example possible with `mdmb` [@mdmb; @grundMImdmb], could improve comparability and help isolate differences attributable to modeling choices rather than implementation details.
In addition, the present study relied on simulated data that satisfy the assumed model conditions (e.g., normality and homoscedasticity of residuals). In applied settings, these assumptions are often violated. It would therefore be informative to investigate the behavior of the methods using real data or under conditions of model misspecification. Moreover, the simulated missing data mechanisms did not include missing not at random (MNAR) processes, which are likely to occur in practice and may further affect method performance.  
Overall, the present findings provide a starting point for understanding the behavior of missing data methods in small-sample multilevel settings, but further research is required to assess their robustness under more complex and realistic conditions.
